jsnvu6-e179853-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 4: whether habit contributes anything to the facility of an act, referring to Cajetan.

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e117.summary: Argument that habit produces facility: what is done more pleasurably is done more easily, and after a habit is generated the act is elicited with more pleasure (Ethics).
claims: Acts after habit are more pleasurable and hence easier (objection)

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e130.summary: Second argument: all difficulty arises from resistance, and an object less disagreeable to the appetite resists less; a good habit makes the good of reason appear less disagreeable, as shown earlier; so it makes the act easier.
claims: Difficulty arises from resistance of the object
Good habit makes the good of reason appear less disagreeable

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e147.summary: Argument for the opposite: virtue concerns the good and difficult; if habit removed the difficulty it would harm rather than help, as it would diminish the act's goodness and merit.
claims: If habit removed difficulty it would diminish merit (counter-argument)

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e160.summary: Outline of the response: first, whether facility is a condition of the act or of the agent; second, whether such facility comes from habit; third, a corollary.

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e173.summary: Facility is a relational condition between agent and act and can arise either solely from the act and object—as for the same person carrying fifty pounds is easy and a hundred hard, or for the virtuous abstaining is easier than enduring pain (Ethics III)—or solely from the agent, as a strong person carries ten pounds more easily than a weak one.
claims: Facility is a relation of agent to act
Facility can derive from the act and object or from the agent's disposition

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e212.summary: The facility at issue—greater ease with the same species of act after a habit than before—arises wholly from the agent's disposition and is a mode of the agent, not of the act. First proof: when two acts are entirely alike in everything intrinsic, yet one is easier, the difference must lie wholly in the agent; and acts before and after a habit are sometimes entirely alike.
claims: Facility produced by habit is wholly a condition of the agent, not the act
Acts before and after a habit can be wholly alike

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e247.summary: Rebuts the objection that acts after habit are always more intense: this is not universally true, and even if it were it would confirm the point, since a more intense act is in itself harder; so any added facility must come from the agent. Second proof: facility of the work diminishes merit, so if habit made facility a condition of the work, it would diminish merit, which is false.
claims: Acts after a habit are not always more intense
A more intense act is of itself more difficult
Habit does not diminish merit, so its facility is not a condition of the work
concepts: facility of the work vs. agent

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e278.summary: How habit causes facility: difficulty in cognitive and appetitive acts arises from the object being presented under mixed aspects of true and false or good and evil. An object presented as purely good or purely evil is pursued or fled without difficulty, but mixed voluntary cases (e.g. jettisoning cargo in a storm) are chosen with difficulty and sorrow. Whatever diminishes one aspect makes the choice easier. Moral habits do this because the acts that generate them alter bodily dispositions, so that pleasures, such as venereal ones, become or appear less fitting to the temperate; thus what was fled with difficulty before is fled easily after.
claims: Difficulty arises from objects presented under mixed aspects of good and evil
Moral habits produce facility by altering bodily disposition so that objects appear less fitting
Mixed voluntary choices are made with difficulty and sorrow

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e351.summary: The same holds for cognitive habits: self-evident first principles are assented to without difficulty, but propositions whose terms admit doubt or admixture of falsity are assented to only with labor through various middles; once the truth is found and a habit formed by repeated assent, we assent readily, no longer hesitating, because we recall the prior discussion and assent.
claims: Cognitive habits produce facility of assent by recalling prior resolution and repeated assent
First principles are assented to without difficulty

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e382.summary: Corollary resolving the overarching question whether habit contributes to the substance of the act or only its mode: the act has only two modes, intensity and determination, neither really distinct from the act's essence; facility is a mode of the agent, not the act. Since habit per se contributes to neither mode, nor to the essence, and facility belongs to the agent, habit's contribution to facility does not imply any contribution to the act's essence.
claims: The only modes of an act are intensity and determination, not really distinct from its essence
Facility is a mode of the agent, not of the act
Habit contributes per se neither to the act's essence nor to its modes

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e417.summary: Reply to the first two arguments: they rightly show that habit makes an act easier to elicit, but all the facility lies in the disposition habit places in the agent, not in the act.
claims: Habit's facility resides in the agent's disposition

jsnvu6-e179853-d1e430.summary: On the argument for the opposite: it rightly concludes that if habit's facility were a condition of the act, habit would harm more than help by diminishing merit, which is conceded.
claims: Were facility a condition of the act, habit would diminish merit

jsnvu6-e179853.summary: Question 4 completes the series on habit and the act by asking whether habit contributes to facility. Durandus first locates facility as a relation between agent and act that can derive either from the act and object (carrying fifty versus a hundred pounds) or from the agent (the strong versus the weak). The facility gained through habit belongs wholly to the agent, since acts before and after the habit can be wholly alike, more intense acts are of themselves harder, and facility of the work would diminish merit. Habit produces this facility by removing the mixture of opposed aspects that makes acts difficult. Moral habits alter bodily dispositions so that objects appear more or less fitting, and cognitive habits let us recall earlier resolution and assent. A corollary settles the overarching question: an act has only two modes, intensity and determination, neither really distinct from its essence, and habit contributes per se to neither. Facility is a mode of the agent, so habit's real contribution lies in the agent's disposition, not in the substance of the act.
claims: Facility produced by habit is a condition of the agent, not of the act
Habits produce facility by removing mixed aspects of good/evil or true/false in the object
Moral habits work by altering bodily dispositions
Habit contributes per se neither to the substance of an act nor to its modes of intensity and determination
